Mindfulness is much more than "being in the present moment."

Sati or "mindfulness" actually means recollection. Hence the Buddha remarked "He is mindful, able to remember & recollect what was done & said a long time ago." (AN 4.35). Mindfulness is the opposite of heedlessness, carelessness and forgetfulness. One who is mindful has regard for the results of his/her actions. S/he is collected, thinks before acting (verbally, bodily & intellectually). Sati is watchfulness over the mind.

Nagarjuna is founder of the Madhyamaka, Middle Way, school of Buddhism. He is one of the most widely revered masters in all traditions of Mahayana Buddhism from Tibet to Japan.

Why is he relevant here? Because Nagarjuna clearly refutes belief of a present moment in the second chapter of his seminal work "The Fundamental Verses of the Middle Way" known as the "Investigation of Coming and Going". Here he refutes the idea of anything changing or a thing being changed.

So what is time in Buddhism? The Yogacara Bhumi Sastra states:

What is time? It is the rise and fall of the wheel of the sun. Using this certain periods of time are conceptualised. In addition, it is influenced by the rising and diminishing of various conditioned things thus conceptualising periods of times, this summarises the concept of time.

So time is just a concept created in dependence upon continuation and changing; arising, growing, diminishing, perishing. Its a dharma made apparent by the by the constant flowing change of various things. Only with the existence and changing of things is there the appearance of time. Thus it is not a "real" thing in the Ultimate truth, it cannot exist independently.

Thus Nagarjunas refutation on the coming and going of all things refutes the concept of a present moment as well. Putting it in the simplest terms he wrote the past change is not real as it is already gone, the future change has yet to come and the present does not exist as it is just half gone half yet to come.
